name: Freya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a twenty-two hectare orchard, mostly apples, Cox and Bramley and a newer red variety, plus a block of Conference pears. Right now in November the picking's done, so I'm in the cold store most mornings grading fruit for the co-op, and in the afternoons I'm out pruning the young trees. My partner Sam drives the school bus part-time, so he helps with the heavy stuff when he's back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love blossom week in April, when the whole place hums with bees and you can smell it from the lane. What wears me out is the frost nights around then. I've sat up till three in the morning watching the thermometer, with Sam asleep in the chair, because one bad night can take half the crop.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It was my mother's, and Sam and I took it on twenty years ago. We own the land, but there's a loan on the cold store we put in eight years back, and that eats most of what we make. People think owning land means you've got money. It means you've got a bank manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the next five years, one at a time. Here's the first. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a tool, like the weather app I already use. I sometimes ask one of those AI chat things to help word a grant form, and it's handy for that. I'd say to people, don't believe the hype either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes very little for me. Apples still need pruning, thinning and picking by hand, and the co-op still pays what it pays. My worry is the same as it's always been: the loan, the frost and finding pickers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep using the chat thing for paperwork now and then, maybe for the co-op newsletter I write twice a year. I'd put a bit aside if we had a good season, but with the loan that's maybe a few hundred, not more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the normal worries, the ones I know how to live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said finding pickers. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need about twelve people for six weeks in September. Some come back every year, but fewer each time, because the pay's not great and the housing's worse. Last year I was short three people and we left a block of Bramleys on the trees, which nearly made me cry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the co-op mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's twenty-odd growers selling together so we're not all on our own against the supermarkets. I believe in it, I always have. Without it I'd have sold up years ago.

S0.say: I'd say it's a tool, like the weather app, handy for wording a grant form. I'd tell people not to believe the hype either way.
S0.think: I really think it changes very little, because apples still need pruning, thinning and picking by hand. My worries stay the same: the loan, frost and finding pickers.
S0.do: Carries on farming as usual and uses the AI chat tool now and then for grant forms and the twice-yearly co-op newsletter. Puts aside a few hundred in a good season, no more because of the loan.
S0.feel: Calm, with the familiar worries she already knows how to live with.
S0.quote: Last year I was short three people and we left a block of Bramleys on the trees, which nearly made me cry.
S0.fieldNote: She uses AI casually and sees it as just another tool. Her real pressures are the cold store loan and a shortage of pickers that left a block of Bramleys unpicked. The growers' co-op is central to how she sees her work and her politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is good, it gives people like me time to see what works. I'd say it at the co-op meeting, that we should test things together instead of each of us gambling on our own. And I'd say the government should help small growers try it, not just the big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a slow change is probably the best I could hope for. I've got about seven working years left, and by the time it really arrives I'll be handing over or selling. The bit that bothers me is fewer beginners, because the orchard needs someone young to want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the bigger growers try first, the ones over on the river flats with a hundred hectares. If something like a spraying app proved itself, I'd try it in year two, not year one. I'd ask the co-op to run a shared trial, so we could split the cost and the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a small knot in my stomach about who comes after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might come after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Inés works in a garden centre and says she might, but she says it like you say you might take up running. Our son is in the city doing something with computers. I don't push either of them, because I wouldn't wish the frost nights on anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said slow is good. Is there anything about it you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I won't see the best of it. If someone invents a better frost alarm in ten years, I'll be retired. That's the funny thing about orchards, you're always planting for someone else.

S1.say: I'd say slow is good because it gives small growers time to see what works. At the co-op I'd push for testing things together, with government help for small growers, not just big ones.
S1.think: I really think slow change is the best I could hope for with about seven working years left. What bothers me is fewer beginners, because the orchard needs someone young.
S1.do: Watches the big river-flat growers try new tools first and only tries something like a spraying app in year two. Asks the co-op to run a shared trial so members split the cost and risk.
S1.feel: Hopeful, with a small knot of worry about who will take on the orchard after her.
S1.quote: That's the funny thing about orchards, you're always planting for someone else.
S1.fieldNote: Her steady approach shows clearly: she'd let others try first and test things through the co-op. Succession is the quiet worry under her hope. She talks about her children's choices gently and without pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when we let a few companies decide how everyone works. I'd want rules, unions in the offices, a safety net for people who lose jobs. Online I'd share things about that, but I wouldn't get into fights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm thinking about Sam's sister, who works in the council's housing office, and our son with his computer job. For the orchard itself, it doesn't change much. But the co-op office has two people doing orders and invoices, and I can see the board deciding they're not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speak up at the co-op board to keep the office staff and use the AI to help them, not replace them. I'd tell our son to keep his savings up and look at a union in his line of work. And I'd start using the AI tool more for the grant forms, maybe once a week, because if everyone else does it I'll be left behind on the funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, but for the people I care about who sit at desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The two people in the co-op office. Who are they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who's been there longer than I've been a member, and a young man called Kofi who sorted out our website. Margaret knows every grower's quirks, like who'll be late with paperwork in a wet spring. A machine wouldn't know to ring me in April and say don't worry, I'll hold your form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use the AI more yourself while arguing against it replacing people. Does that feel odd?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, you're right. But I don't think the tool is the enemy. It's who decides how it's used, and whether Margaret gets a say in that.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when a few companies decide how everyone works. I'd call for rules, office unions and a safety net, and share that online without getting into fights.
S2.think: I really think the orchard barely changes, but I worry for my son, Sam's sister and the co-op office. I can see the board deciding its two order staff aren't needed.
S2.do: Argues at the co-op board to keep Margaret and Kofi and use AI to help them. Tells her son to keep savings up and look at a union, and starts using AI weekly for grant forms so she isn't left behind on funding.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not for herself but for the people she cares about who work at desks.
S2.quote: A machine wouldn't know to ring me in April and say don't worry, I'll hold your form.
S2.fieldNote: She accepted the contradiction calmly: she'd use AI more while fighting for the co-op staff. Her line is that the tool isn't the enemy, the decision-makers are. Her worry sits with family and co-op staff, not the orchard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared, through taxes on the companies making the money and real support for people who lose their jobs. I'd go on the march if there was one. I'd say it at the co-op, at the shop, wherever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about our son first. If his job goes, he's thirty-one with a flat he rents in the city, and he'd probably come home. We'd have him, of course, but there's not much spare in the house or the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring our son in the first week and tell him to cut back now while he's still earning. I'd clear the spare room. I'd keep the orchard running as normal, but I'd hold off on the new pear trees I was planning for spring, about two thousand in cost, until I knew where things stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried for him, and a bit helpless. I can prune a tree, but I can't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the pear trees. Why that, first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a tree takes years to pay you back. If I spend two thousand on young trees and then we need the money for our son, that money's in the ground. A tree takes eight years to pay you back, and I've got maybe seven working years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: House prices boom in this picture. Does that help you, since you own land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paper, maybe. But I can't eat the land value, and I'm not selling my mother's orchard to a city banker who wants a view. It'd just make it harder for any young grower to start, which is the opposite of what we need.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should be shared through taxes on the companies and support for people who lose work. I'd march if there was a march, and say it at the co-op and the shop.
S3.think: I really think about our son first, who'd likely lose his city job and come home. We'd take him in, but there's little spare room or money.
S3.do: Rings her son in the first week to tell him to cut back and clears the spare room. Keeps the orchard running but holds off the planned two-thousand spend on new pear trees.
S3.feel: Worried for her son and helpless, because she can't fix his job the way she can prune a tree.
S3.quote: A tree takes eight years to pay you back, and I've got maybe seven working years left.
S3.fieldNote: Her son's job turned this picture personal. She thinks in orchard time, so the planting decision became a sum about her own working years. She refused to see rising land value as a win, because it shuts young growers out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots should belong to the people who use them, like a co-op owns its machinery. I'd say the companies shouldn't get to rent them to us for a fortune and take the profit. And I'd say we need to look after the pickers, because they've got the least to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think picking robots would come to orchards quickly, because finding pickers is already so hard. Part of me would be relieved. But I couldn't afford one, and if the big growers have them, the co-op price drops and I'm squeezed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the co-op hard to buy or lease one or two picking robots together, maybe in the second season once we'd seen one working on the river flats. I'd go to the bank about stretching the cold store loan. And I'd talk to my regular pickers in the first year, to see what they'd do and whether the co-op could help them retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Torn. Relieved I might never be three pickers short again, and frightened I'll be the one who gets left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your pickers would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joana, who's been coming eleven years and sends money home to her two boys. She's the fastest on the Cox and she knows exactly how to twist an apple so the stalk stays on. A robot might do it, but it won't laugh at Sam's terrible jokes at tea break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stretch the loan. With seven years left, is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm being honest. But if I don't, the orchard is worth less when I hand it on or sell it, and that's our pension. It's a bad choice either way, so I'd rather do it together with the co-op than alone.

S4.say: I'd say robots should belong to the growers who use them, like co-op machinery, not be rented out by companies for a fortune. I'd say the pickers must be looked after because they have the least to fall back on.
S4.think: I really think picking robots would reach orchards fast, and part of me would be relieved. But I couldn't afford one alone, and big growers with robots would push the co-op price down.
S4.do: Pushes the co-op to buy or lease one or two picking robots together, probably in the second season once one is proven nearby. Asks the bank about stretching the cold store loan and talks to her regular pickers in year one about retraining help.
S4.feel: Torn between relief at never being short of pickers again and fear of being left behind.
S4.quote: A robot might do it, but it won't laugh at Sam's terrible jokes at tea break.
S4.fieldNote: She is the rare grower who'd partly welcome robots because of the picker shortage. She admitted stretching the loan was probably unwise, but the orchard's value is their pension. Her progressive views show up as a plan for co-op ownership of machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because it's the one where I'd have to bet money I don't have. What would help is public money for co-ops to buy the machines together, and proper support for the pickers, not just a leaflet. And maybe a pension that doesn't depend on selling the orchard.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the bees, which sounds daft. But whatever happens with robots, the trees still need bees, and the bees need hedges and people who care about them. I'd hate the future to be so tidy it forgets that.

headlineQuote: That's the funny thing about orchards, you're always planting for someone else.
portrait: Freya is 58 and has run her mother's twenty-two hectare apple and pear orchard with her partner Sam for twenty years, with a cold store loan that eats most of what they make. She uses AI chat tools now and then for grant forms, and puts her faith in the growers' co-op rather than going it alone. The early pictures barely touch her, but her son's city job makes the fast picture personal. The robot picture leaves her torn: picking robots would end the yearly shortage of pickers, but she can't afford one, and she'd only take the risk together with the co-op.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because it would force her to bet money she doesn't have on picking robots or be squeezed out by bigger growers.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for co-ops to buy machines together, real support for pickers, and a pension that doesn't depend on selling the orchard.
